inline_comments.comment: `escapeHtml` duplicates sanitization logic that already exists in `packages/mermaid/src/diagrams/common/common.ts` via `sanitizeText()` (backed by DOMPurify). Introducing a bespoke escape function on the class makes it a private implementation detail of `ClassDB` rather than a shared utility, and it is less robust than DOMPurify. Per project convention, shared rendering helpers belong in `common.ts`. Consider replacing `this.escapeHtml(title)` with a call to the existing `sanitizeText(title, getConfig())`, or at minimum extracting `escapeHtml` to `common.ts` so that `flowDb.ts` (which has the same need) can also reuse it.

The inline `.style('background', '#ffffde')` and `.style('border', '1px solid #333')` hardcode colours instead of honouring the active theme. `flowchart/styles.ts` (and its siblings) already define `div.mermaidTooltip { background: ${options.tertiaryColor}; border: 1px solid ${options.border2}; ... }`. Because inline `style` attributes have higher specificity than class-based CSS rules, these JS-applied values silently override the theme variables for every theme. The same block also omits `font-family`, which the CSS rule supplies via `${options.fontFamily}`, so the tooltip will render in the browser's default font. The entire inline-style chain should be removed so that the existing stylesheet is solely responsible for visual presentation.

The selector was widened from `svg.selectAll('g.node')` to `svg.selectAll('g').filter(...)`, which selects every `<g>` in the SVG that carries a `title` attribute. This is considerably broader: SVG structural elements such as subgraph containers, edge path groups, marker groups, and cluster wrappers may also have `title` attributes and will now receive unexpected mouseover/mouseout listeners, triggering tooltip display for non-node elements. A more precise approach is `svg.selectAll('g.node[title]')` (or `g.node[title], g.classGroup[title]` if class diagram groups also need coverage), which keeps specificity close to the original without requiring a manual `.filter()` pass over the entire element tree.

The original vertical offset expression was `window.scrollY + rect.top - 14 + document.body.scrollTop`. The new expression is `window.scrollY + rect.bottom + 4`, which silently drops `document.body.scrollTop`. These are not always equivalent: on pages where `<body>` is itself the overflow scroll container (e.g. `body { overflow: auto; height: 100vh }`), `document.body.scrollTop` carries the real scroll offset while `window.scrollY` may be 0, meaning the tooltip will be mispositioned. Per the project rule on DOM scroll-offset arithmetic, the equivalence must be verified across all scroll states and the reasoning documented inline. If the removal is intentional (e.g. it is always zero in the relevant browsers), add a brief inline comment explaining why.

Per project coding standards, use `// @ts-expect-error: <reason>` instead of `// @ts-ignore`. `@ts-expect-error` causes a compile error if the suppression becomes unnecessary (e.g. after a type upgrade), whereas `@ts-ignore` silently persists forever. The comment should also explain what type mismatch is being suppressed so future maintainers can evaluate whether the workaround is still warranted.

This block unconditionally appends a new `.mermaidTooltip` `<div>` to `<body>` on every call to `setupToolTips`, which is invoked on every render via `bindFunctions()`. There is no existence guard (unlike the `.empty()` check used correctly in the `classDb.ts` changes). As a result: (1) repeated renders accumulate orphaned tooltip divs, causing visual artifacts and a DOM/memory leak; (2) because the `let tooltipElem` variable is reassigned here *after* the mouseover/mouseout handlers already closed over it, the handlers will reference this newly created element while the element created (or selected) at the top of the function—which may also be in the DOM—goes unused. Add an `.empty()` guard, and move the creation block to the top of the function (where `classDb.ts` correctly places it), removing the `// @ts-ignore` at the same time.

Same hardcoded-colour issue as in `classDb.ts`: `#ffffde` and `#333` override the theme-aware values (`${options.tertiaryColor}`, `${options.border2}`) already defined in `flowchart/styles.ts`. These inline styles also omit `font-family`. Since the CSS rule is already injected by the diagram styles pipeline, the inline style block is redundant and should be removed entirely.

general_comments.comment: The tooltip inline-style block is copy-pasted verbatim between `classDb.ts` and `flowDb.ts`, and a functionally identical CSS rule is already emitted by `flowchart/styles.ts` (and analogous `styles.ts`/`styles.js` files in `user-journey` and `block`). The `.mermaidTooltip` CSS class is therefore the canonical source of truth for tooltip presentation. The correct fix is to remove all the inline `.style(...)` chains from both JS files entirely — the existing CSS rules handle layout and appearance, and they correctly use theme variables (`tertiaryColor`, `border2`, `fontFamily`). If the tooltip div is being created before the diagram stylesheet is injected, the right solution is to adjust injection ordering, not to duplicate styles in JS with hardcoded non-theme values.

No unit or end-to-end tests accompany this fix (explicitly noted as unchecked in the PR checklist). The root cause — `this.getBoundingClientRect()` being called on the class instance instead of the DOM element — is a real correctness bug, and the scroll-offset arithmetic change is a potentially observable behaviour difference. Per project rules, every modified conditional branch in rendering logic must be covered by at least one e2e or snapshot test. A Cypress `imgSnapshotTest` or a DOM-level test asserting tooltip position relative to a hovered node would both serve as a regression guard here.

The PR conflates at least three distinct changes: (1) the actual bug fix (`event.currentTarget` vs `this.getBoundingClientRect()`), (2) a design decision to display the tooltip below rather than above the element, and (3) style additions that conflict with the existing CSS. Separating these into focused commits (or PRs) would make the true correctness fix easier to review and revert independently from the cosmetic/design changes.
